paraphrases: A growing number of educators argue that universities ought to replace written examinations with project-based assessment.
It has been suggested that projects, rather than traditional tests, should be the main way of grading university students.
Some people believe that higher education institutions should stop relying on written exams and judge students by the projects they complete.
BE1.stance_reason_th: ฝั่งไม่เห็นด้วยเขียนง่ายและหนักแน่นกว่า เพราะมีเหตุผลชัดเจนเรื่องการวัดความสามารถรายบุคคล (งานกลุ่มมีคนไม่ช่วยงาน และปัจจุบันมี AI ช่วยทำงาน) และเรื่องความเท่าเทียม เพราะโครงงานต้องใช้เวลา อุปกรณ์ และเงิน ส่วนข้อดีของโครงงาน เช่น ฝึกทักษะการทำงานเป็นทีม สามารถยอมรับสั้นๆ แล้วหักล้างว่าควรปรับข้อสอบให้ดีขึ้นและใช้โครงงานเป็นส่วนเสริม ไม่ใช่ยกเลิกการสอบ

agree.reason: Projects assess practical skills that examinations cannot measure.
agree.explain: Real jobs require teamwork, research, planning and presentation, which a timed paper does not test.
agree.example: Engineering students who design and build a small water filter for a village learn skills that they will use directly in their careers.

agree.reason: Projects encourage deep understanding instead of short-term memorisation.
agree.explain: Students have to apply ideas over several weeks, so they remember them for longer.
agree.example: Many students memorise definitions the night before an exam and forget them a week later, but they still remember a research project they completed in their second year.

agree.reason: Projects reduce the stress of a single high-stakes test.
agree.explain: Marks are spread over a longer period, so one bad day does not ruin a student's grade.
agree.example: A student who is ill on the day of a final examination may lose half of the course grade, whereas a project allows time to recover.

disagree.reason: Examinations measure individual knowledge more reliably.
disagree.explain: In group projects, some members do little work, and AI tools can produce polished reports, so the grade may not reflect the student's own ability.
disagree.example: A pharmacy student who must calculate a safe drug dose in an examination hall cannot rely on a classmate or a chatbot.

disagree.reason: Examinations are fairer to students from different backgrounds.
disagree.explain: Projects often require time, transport, equipment and money, which some students do not have.
disagree.example: A student who works part-time in a restaurant every evening has less time for a long project than a classmate supported by wealthy parents.

disagree.reason: Examinations are more efficient and consistent to mark.
disagree.explain: Every student answers the same questions, so lecturers can compare answers using the same criteria.
disagree.example: A lecturer teaching a first-year course of 300 students can mark an exam fairly, but grading 300 different projects consistently would be almost impossible.

outline.intro: Paraphrase: A growing number of educators argue that universities ought to replace written examinations with project-based assessment. Thesis: I disagree because examinations measure individual knowledge more reliably and treat all students under equal conditions.
outline.body1: Reason 1: It is hard to know who really did the work in a project (free-riders in groups, AI tools); example of a pharmacy student calculating a drug dose in an examination hall.
outline.body2: Reason 2: Examinations are fairer because projects need time, transport and money; concession that exams encourage memorisation and ignore teamwork, plus rebuttal (design better exams and use projects alongside them).
outline.conclusion: Restate that projects should complement, not replace, examinations; summarise reliability and fairness; universities should improve exams rather than discard them.

model: In recent years, a growing number of educators have argued that universities ought to replace written examinations with project-based assessment. Although projects certainly have a place in higher education, I disagree that they should take the place of examinations, because examinations measure individual knowledge more reliably and treat every student under equal conditions.

The main weakness of project-based assessment is that it is difficult to tell how much of the work genuinely belongs to each student. In group projects, one or two committed members often carry the rest of the team, yet everyone receives the same grade. Furthermore, now that generative AI tools are freely available, a polished report may reflect a student's skill with software rather than their understanding of the subject. A written examination, by contrast, requires students to recall, apply and explain ideas on their own within a fixed time. For example, a pharmacy student who must calculate a safe drug dose in an examination hall cannot rely on a classmate or a chatbot, and this is precisely the kind of independent competence that patients will later depend on.

Examinations are also fairer to students from different backgrounds. Successful projects frequently require time, transport, equipment and sometimes money, which students who work part-time or live far from campus may lack. A student who serves tables in a restaurant every evening simply cannot spend as many hours on a project as a classmate supported by wealthy parents. In an examination, however, every candidate answers the same questions with the same resources. Admittedly, examinations can encourage memorisation and fail to assess practical skills such as teamwork and presentation. Nevertheless, this is an argument for designing better examinations, with case studies and problem-solving questions, and for using projects alongside them, not for abandoning written tests altogether.

In conclusion, while projects can usefully complement traditional assessment, they should not replace written examinations. Examinations remain the most dependable way to confirm what each individual student knows, and they give all students an equal opportunity to demonstrate it. Universities should therefore improve their examinations rather than discard them.

agree.reason: Smartphones are a major source of distraction in class.
agree.explain: Notifications from games and social media interrupt students' concentration and reduce learning.
agree.example: A teacher may notice students checking LINE messages under their desks during a mathematics lesson and missing key explanations.

agree.reason: Phones make cyberbullying and cheating easier at school.
agree.explain: Students can secretly take photos of classmates or share answers during tests.
agree.example: A student may photograph a classmate in an embarrassing moment and post it in a group chat before the teacher knows.

agree.reason: A ban encourages face-to-face social interaction.
agree.explain: Without phones, students talk and play with each other during breaks.
agree.example: In schools without phones, students are more likely to play football or chat in the canteen than sit silently scrolling.

disagree.reason: Smartphones are valuable learning tools when used properly.
disagree.explain: Students can search for information, check vocabulary, record experiments and submit work online.
disagree.example: In a provincial school with an outdated computer room, a student's own phone may be the only device that gives fast access to online resources.

disagree.reason: Students need to learn how to manage technology responsibly.
disagree.explain: A ban only removes phones for a few hours; it does not teach self-control.
disagree.example: A student whose phone is confiscated all day may still spend the whole evening on TikTok without any guidance.

disagree.reason: Phones are important for safety and communication with parents.
disagree.explain: Parents need to contact children about travel, emergencies or changes to plans.
disagree.example: A student who travels home by songthaew after an evening activity can call a parent if the vehicle is late.

outline.intro: Paraphrase: Many people believe that the simplest solution to classroom distraction is to ban smartphones from schools entirely. Thesis: I disagree with a complete ban, as clear rules are more practical and more educational than prohibition.
outline.body1: Reason 1: Phones are valuable learning tools; example of provincial Thai schools with small, outdated computer rooms.
outline.body2: Reason 2: Students need to learn to manage technology; suggestion of rules (phones in bags during lessons); concession on distraction and cyberbullying plus rebuttal (problems of unregulated use, solved by rules and digital literacy).
outline.conclusion: Restate that a ban is a quick fix that ignores educational value and responsible habits; recommend carefully designed rules.

model: Smartphones have become almost inseparable from the lives of teenagers, and many parents and teachers now believe that the simplest solution to classroom distraction is to ban them from schools entirely. While I understand this concern, I disagree with a complete ban, as I believe that clear rules on when phones may be used are both more practical and more educational than prohibition.

The first reason is that smartphones, when used properly, are valuable learning tools. Students can look up unfamiliar vocabulary, record science experiments, submit assignments online and take part in interactive classroom quizzes. A biology class, for instance, can photograph plants in the school garden and identify them with a free app during the same lesson. In many provincial schools in Thailand, where computer rooms are small and often out of date, a student's own phone may be the only device that gives them fast access to online resources. Removing phones completely would therefore deprive these students of opportunities that their urban peers take for granted.

Another consideration is that young people need to learn how to manage technology, not simply avoid it. If schools confiscate phones for seven hours a day, students will still spend the evening on social media without any guidance on self-control. A more effective approach would be to require phones to be kept in bags during lessons and to allow their use only for specific tasks set by the teacher. It is true that phones can distract students and expose them to cyberbullying, and some schools have reported calmer classrooms after introducing bans. However, these problems stem from unregulated use, and they can largely be addressed through consistent rules and digital literacy lessons rather than a blanket prohibition.

In conclusion, banning smartphones in schools may appear to be a quick fix, but it ignores both their educational value and students' need to develop responsible habits. Carefully designed rules, enforced consistently by all teachers, would allow schools to limit distraction while still preparing students for a world in which digital devices are unavoidable.

disagree.reason: Working from home saves time and money.

outline.intro: Paraphrase: Working from home is often presented as a benefit that all employees welcome. Thesis: I agree that for young employees remote work does more harm than good, because it limits professional learning and weakens career relationships.
outline.body1: Reason 1: Young employees lose informal learning from senior colleagues; example of a junior accountant in Khon Kaen who joins a firm remotely.
outline.body2: Reason 2: Remote work isolates young people and makes them less visible for promotion; concession on saving commuting time and money plus rebuttal (short-term gains vs. long-term losses).
outline.conclusion: Restate that the costs outweigh the benefits; recommend that new staff spend most of the week in the office.

model: Since the pandemic, working from home has become a normal arrangement in many companies, and it is often presented as a benefit that all employees welcome. However, I agree that for young employees in particular, remote work does more harm than good, because it limits their professional learning and weakens the relationships on which their future careers depend.

The most serious drawback is that young employees lose the informal learning that happens naturally in an office. Much of what new graduates need to know is never written in a manual; they acquire it by listening to how senior colleagues handle a difficult client, asking quick questions at the next desk or being invited to observe a meeting. When everyone works from home, these opportunities largely disappear, and even a simple question may require a scheduled video call. Consider a junior accountant in Khon Kaen who joins a firm remotely: she may complete her tasks correctly, yet after a year she is likely to understand far less about how the business actually operates than a colleague who sat beside experienced staff every day.

In addition, remote work can isolate young people at a stage of life when they are building professional networks. Promotions and new opportunities often depend on being noticed by managers, and employees who are rarely seen in person can easily be overlooked. Loneliness is also a genuine risk for graduates who have moved to a new city and live alone. Admittedly, working from home saves commuting time and money, which matters to young people on modest salaries. Even so, these savings are short-term gains, whereas the skills and connections lost in the first years of a career can affect a person's progress for decades.

In conclusion, although working from home offers convenience, its costs for young employees clearly outweigh its benefits. Companies should therefore ensure that new staff spend most of their working week in the office, where they can learn from colleagues and build the relationships that support long-term success.

outline.intro: Paraphrase: The countries affected by climate change differ enormously in responsibility and capacity. Thesis: I strongly agree that wealthy nations should contribute more, on the grounds of historical responsibility and greater financial resources.
outline.body1: Reason 1: Historical responsibility - industrialised countries have emitted for over a century and built their prosperity on it; example of a farmer in rural Laos or Bangladesh.
outline.body2: Reason 2: Rich countries have greater capacity, while poorer nations still need basic services; concession that some fast-growing economies are major emitters plus rebuttal (contributions should be proportionate, which still means rich countries pay more).
outline.conclusion: Restate that rich countries should pay a larger share; summarise responsibility and capacity; support is fairness, not charity.

model: Climate change is a global problem, but the countries affected by it differ enormously in both their responsibility for it and their capacity to respond. For this reason, I strongly agree that wealthy nations should contribute more than developing countries to the fight against climate change, on the grounds of their historical responsibility and their far greater financial resources.

The first argument concerns responsibility. Industrialised countries in Europe and North America have been burning coal, oil and gas on a large scale for well over a century, so a substantial share of the carbon dioxide now in the atmosphere was released by them. Their present prosperity was, in effect, built on these emissions. Developing countries, by contrast, have only recently begun to industrialise, and their emissions per person often remain much lower. It would therefore be unjust to expect a rice farmer in rural Laos or Bangladesh to bear the same burden as a citizen of a country whose wealth was created through decades of pollution.

Equally important is the question of capacity. Rich countries have the money, technology and expertise to invest in renewable energy, while many poorer nations are still struggling to provide basic electricity, clean water and healthcare. If the cost of reducing emissions were shared equally, developing countries would be forced to choose between protecting the climate and lifting their citizens out of poverty. Admittedly, some fast-growing economies are now major emitters, and it is reasonable to expect them to play a larger role. Nevertheless, this does not cancel the greater obligation of wealthy nations; it simply means that contributions should be fair and proportionate to each country's means.

In conclusion, rich countries should pay a larger share of the cost of tackling climate change, since they are largely responsible for the problem and are best equipped to address it. Such support is not charity but a fair recognition that a shared crisis requires each nation to contribute according to its history and ability.

agree.reason: Prevention is more cost-effective than treatment.

agree.reason: Prevention protects people's quality of life.

agree.reason: Early detection reduces pressure on hospitals.

outline.intro: Paraphrase: Every government must divide a limited health budget between treating people who are ill and preventing illness. Thesis: Governments should give greater priority to prevention because it saves money and protects the quality of life of the whole population.
outline.body1: Reason 1: Prevention is cost-effective compared with treating chronic diseases such as diabetes and kidney failure; example of Thai village health volunteers checking blood pressure.
outline.body2: Reason 2: Prevention keeps people healthy so they can work and care for families (vaccination, clean water, road safety); concession that sick people cannot be abandoned plus rebuttal (prevention eases pressure on hospitals).
outline.conclusion: Restate firm support for prevention; summarise cost, wellbeing and benefit to the treatment system; a wise health policy keeps citizens healthy.

model: Every government must decide how to divide a limited health budget between treating people who are already ill and preventing illness from developing in the first place. In my view, governments should give greater priority to prevention, because it saves money in the long term and protects the quality of life of the whole population.

The most persuasive argument for prevention is its cost-effectiveness. Treating chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart disease and kidney failure is extremely expensive, as patients may need medication, hospital care and even dialysis for many years. By contrast, programmes that encourage regular exercise, reduce salt and sugar consumption or screen people for high blood pressure cost relatively little per person. In Thailand, for instance, village health volunteers who visit homes, check blood pressure and remind elderly residents to take their medicine can identify problems early, long before an expensive hospital admission becomes necessary. Money spent at this early stage therefore goes much further than the same amount spent in an intensive care unit.

Prevention also benefits society in ways that treatment cannot. Vaccination campaigns, clean drinking water and road safety measures such as helmet laws stop people from becoming ill or injured at all, which means that they can continue to work, study and care for their families. A father who avoids a stroke, for example, remains able to support his household rather than depending on it. Admittedly, people who are already sick cannot be abandoned, and hospitals need sufficient funding to treat them properly. However, increasing spending on prevention does not mean neglecting patients; on the contrary, as fewer people develop serious diseases, pressure on hospitals will ease, and more resources will be available for each patient who does need care.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that governments should invest more in preventing disease than in treating it. Prevention is cheaper, protects people before they suffer, and ultimately strengthens the treatment system itself. A wise health policy, therefore, is one that keeps citizens healthy rather than simply waiting for them to fall ill.
